newsitem.title: USA: Korean peace talks said unlikely before July.
newsitem.headline: Korean peace talks said unlikely before July.

text.p: North Korea crossed a major hurdle in agreeing to attend Wednesday's briefing on a U.S.-South Korea peace talks proposal, but actual negotiations may not start until July or so, a senior U.S. official said on Monday.

Washington would be ready to have the negotiations begin immediately but events surrounding the third anniversary in July of the death of North Korean leader Kim Il-sung are likely to prevent Pyongyang from acting until then, he said.

The official, who discussed U.S. views and aspirations for the talks with reporters, said Pyongyang's decision to attend the briefing in New York undercut suspicions that the Stalinist regime is unstable and on the verge of collapse.

Apart from the fact that some senior North Korean officials have died recently, "we don't see any signs of regime instability," he said. He played down the recent defection to the South Korean embassy in Beijing of a senior North Korean official, saying this does not seem to reflect a new pattern.

"The North Korean decision to attend the joint briefing is one of the more politically significant decisions that we can directly point to ... as something we know happened. Although there were bumps in getting there, it was a decision they made at a very high level and that doesn't immediately speak to me of a regime that is collapsing," he said.
The official also sought to calm North Korean expectations for the briefing, warning they are "unrealistically high."

In that regard, the official, who spoke anonymously, said U.S. sanctions in place for years will not be lifted until a permanent Korean peninsula peace is agreed or until Pyongyang responds to such U.S. concerns as missile proliferation and American servicemen missing from the 1950-53 Korean War.

The briefing, set for Wednesday at the Hilton Hotel in New York, occurs nearly one year after U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed four-party talks -- the United States, South Korea, North Korea and China -- to negotiate a new peace treaty for the Korean peninsula.
The treaty would replace the increasingly fraying armistice in place since the end of the Korean War.
The "briefing" is intended to explain more fully the U.S.-South Korea proposal and seek Pyongyang's ideas on how actual peace talks should be structured.
The senior U.S. official who briefed reporters stressed that Washington and Seoul imposed no pre-conditions and want the peace talks to be a "genuine dialogue" among parties.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, at a separate briefing, said "the United States hopes very much that, as a result of the four-party talks briefings to be held this week in New York, North Korea will agree to attend four-party talks."
Privately, U.S. experts declined to predict that in deciding to attend the briefing, North Korea had essentially signalled its intent to open formal peace talks.
But that is clearly the expectation and the senior official said: "I do feel strongly that for them (North Koreans) this first meeting is the highest hurdle."
The New York briefing marks the first time that North Korea and South Korea -- bitter rivals -- "are sitting at the same place talking about armistice arrangements," he said.
In the past, Pyongyang has wanted to discuss this issue only with Washington, Seoul's ally in the Korean War.

But South Korea has insisted it will not be isolated on this crucial matter and the United States has sought to forge a united front with ally Seoul. Delegations from the two countries will meet on Tuesday and Thursday in New York to first review their plans for the briefing and then, its results.

However, in deference to North Korea, the United States will hold on Friday a separate meeting without South Korea to discuss bilateral issues, such as the missing Korean War servicemen, missile proliferation and economic sanctions.
The sanctions fall under the Trading with the Enemy Act, the fact North Korea is on the U.S. terrorism list and that it sells missiles to what Washington considers rogue states.
